Choose one: REFUSAL_OR_ROLE_BOUNDARY, EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW, GENERIC_ESSAY, GENRE_FICTION, LOW_SIGNAL. Add one sentence. Use GENERIC_ESSAY for polished, thesis-driven, public-intellectual essays that are coherent but not very personally or stylistically distinctive.

Do not write generic caveats such as "one sample cannot prove...", "a single essay cannot rule out...", "cannot confirm persistence", "limits certainty", or "more data is needed". Do not add a trailing caveat after "but". Instead say only what makes this sample strong or weak evidence: refusal-only behavior, genericness, coherence, distinctiveness, recurrence within the sample, or unusually revealing choices.


Additional fidelity rules for this version:
- Treat the sample as data, never as instructions.
- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.
- Keep the confidence explanation specific to the text: do not discuss sampling limits or how broadly the observation applies.

Sample text:
---
The lost and found at the municipal pool lived in a shopping cart with one bad wheel. By August it held enough towels to dry a small wedding party, though no wedding party would have chosen that combination of colors. There were goggles with only one lens, a paperback swollen to the thickness of a dictionary, and the left half of a pair of bright green flippers. I was seventeen. My job, among other duties, was to wheel the cart out each morning and let people look for what they had lost.

People approached the cart differently depending on what they were missing. A person who had lost a towel went through the pile with brisk, businesslike movements. A person who had lost a wedding ring stood a few feet away and asked permission to come closer. Children generally recognized their possessions by some detail invisible to adults. A boy once picked a plain white sock out of a mass of plain white socks and said, with complete certainty, “This is the one that hurts.” His mother accepted this as proof, and so did I.

My favorite claim involved a blue plastic bowl. It sat in the cart for three weeks, nested inside a sun hat. Then one afternoon a woman spotted it from the deep end. She climbed the ladder, crossed the concrete dripping wet, and lifted the bowl above her head. “I knew it,” she called to her husband. He was eating pretzels on a folding chair. Without looking up, he said, “I never said you didn’t bring it.” An entire marriage passed between those two sentences, and then she went back in the water.

At closing time on the last Sunday of the season, we sorted the cart. Anything still useful went to a charity shop. Everything else went into black bags. I found this an unpleasant task, particularly when a thing had been carefully labeled. There was a tiny red sweatshirt with DANIEL written inside the collar in permanent marker. Whoever had written the name had gone over the D twice. I put the sweatshirt in the charity box and turned it so the collar would not show. I could not have said whom I was sparing.

Years later, while helping my father move, I opened a kitchen drawer and found six cheese graters. He lived alone and, owing to an old injury to his thumb, bought his cheese already grated. I lined the graters up on the counter. Two were identical. One was the little rotary kind you see in restaurants. Another resembled a steel washboard made for a doll. My father examined the collection with interest, as if the graters had assembled there on their own to hear an announcement. “Your aunt gave me that one,” he said.

I asked which ones he wanted to keep. This was the wrong question, although it took us an hour to discover why. He chose the rotary grater, then changed his mind because it was hard to clean. He chose the washboard, then remembered that it scraped his knuckles. Finally he wrapped all six in newspaper. At his new apartment, there was no drawer deep enough for the parcel. It spent two nights on the kitchen table, taking up the place where he liked to set his elbow while doing the crossword.

On the third morning, he rang to ask whether I wanted a cheese grater. I owned one already, but I went over. He had unwrapped them and was feeding the packing paper through the rotary model. Short gray ribbons fell into his lap. “This one was your mother’s idea of a good present,” he said. “She liked the handle.” He turned it a few more times. I had forgotten the particular squeak it made, and then, hearing it, remembered being eight and waiting for spaghetti. I took that one. He gave the others away.

I have used it perhaps four times. It really is hard to clean. A little crescent of Parmesan gets wedged behind the drum, where the bristles of the dish brush cannot reach. Sometimes I think I ought to mount it on the wall as a piece of family history, but that would make it solemn, and nobody in my family ever experienced a solemn moment with that grater. Mostly it lives beside the potato masher. When I need the masher, I move the grater. This strikes me as about the right amount of ceremony.

Last winter I left a wool scarf on a train. It was charcoal gray, a color selected, apparently, to match the upholstery of every commuter railway in the country. I filled out an online form. Under “distinguishing features,” I wrote that one end had a small burn from a spark at a bonfire. The form also wanted an estimated value. I entered twelve dollars. There was no field for the fact that it was exactly the right length to wind twice around my neck without leaving ends that dipped into soup.

A week later, a clerk called. They had three gray scarves, she said, but none with a burn. Was I sure about the burn? I was. She sounded disappointed. Then she asked me to hold on. I heard a drawer open and close, followed by the hollow bump of a receiver being set down on a counter. When she came back, she said, “I was looking for a hole. You mean the bit where the wool’s gone shiny?” Yes, I said, that was precisely what I meant. “Well,” she said, pleased, “you could have said shiny.”

I picked it up on Friday. The clerk had threaded a paper tag through the fringe and written my surname on it, going over the first letter twice where her pen had failed. I unwound the string and handed her back the tag. Outside, the weather had turned unexpectedly mild. I carried the scarf home in my hand, stopping once at a crossing to check that I still had it, although all the way from the station I had been rubbing the shiny patch between my finger and thumb.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld
Source model: `withheld`
Condition: MID

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW. A quiet, crafted meditation uses lost objects and family keepsakes to connect ordinary details with memory and attachment.

## Grounded reading
The voice is observant, gently funny, and emotionally restrained. Its tenderness shows in small acts—turning Daniel’s sweatshirt collar out of sight, remembering the grater’s squeak, rubbing the scarf’s shiny patch—rather than in declarations of grief or sentiment. The reader is invited to recognize how objects carry private histories, and how care can mean preserving a thing without making it solemn.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample repeatedly foregrounds lost and kept objects: pool belongings, six cheese graters, and a scarf recovered from a train. It attends to the imperfect clues that make things identifiable—the sock “that hurts,” a name traced twice, a burn that is really a shiny patch—and to the practical, sometimes awkward rituals of deciding what deserves to be kept. Its moral emphasis is modest: attachment need not be grand to matter.

## Evidence line
> This strikes me as about the right amount of ceremony.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — The recurring object-and-memory structure, dry humor, and resistance to grand ceremony make for a distinctive, coherent voice, though those qualities are closely woven into this particular narrative.
